Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore ⁠through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for ⁠about 30 people ⁠still missing.
Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.
Said Iqbal, ⁠a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the ​implementation of safety protocols was being ‌assessed and that he ‌would summon the factory’s chief executive.
Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have ‌been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.
She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.
The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.
“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”
He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.
Anxious relatives have waited for news outside the burnt-out factory.
The Banten province governor, Andra Soni, said an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The firm employs about 5,000 people and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market. Its ‌products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.
The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. He said the facility had adequate evacuation routes and fire protection systems that complied with applicable safety standards and were functioning at the time of the fire.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others ⁠⁠rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia .
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark , which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture , the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at ⁠⁠environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the ⁠⁠main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement , developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.
Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.
Joeri Rogelj, professor of climate science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.
Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.
“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’
Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.
Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.
Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”
He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”
In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.
Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.
Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”
He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.
The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.
“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.

A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’.
Gaza turned into ‘toxic wasteland’ by Israel’s war, says new report
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.
Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).
“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.
“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”
The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.
It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.
Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.
Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.
In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.
Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.
Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.
Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.
A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.
By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.
The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.
Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.
The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.
The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.
Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.
A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.
According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.
Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.
Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.
Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.
In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.
July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.
By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.
By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.
Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.
These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.
Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.
By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.
Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.
Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.
In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.
The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.
The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.
Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.
Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.
Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.
A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says , external .
Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.
It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

Iran's foreign ministry condemned the US naval blockade as "military aggression" on Monday and said Tehran would use "every means" to counter it, a day after US President Donald Trump threatened to sink Iranian tankers attempting to breach it.
Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, speaking at his weekly press briefing, described the blockade as a violation of the UN Charter and an "act of crime," adding that Tehran considered itself entitled to use any means to defend itself.
"We will certainly not tolerate this situation and will use every means to counter US aggression," Baghaei said.
On Sunday, Trump warned that Iranian ships attempting to break the blockade would be sent to the "bottom of the sea."
Asked about the possibility by a Fox News reporter, he said: "I hope they do it; they'll all go down to the bottom of the sea, just like the rest of their navy."
Media outlets and figures close to the IRGC have called in recent days for a convoy of Iranian oil tankers to be dispatched to break the blockade, with some threatening that Gulf oil facilities would be targeted if the vessels came under attack. Iranian officials have said they have no concrete plan to do so.
IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency published an article on Sunday acknowledging the wave of reports, and said no competent or official authority in the armed forces, the Supreme National Security Council or the government had announced such a plan.
Tasnim said the reports stemmed entirely from proposals put forward by individuals in the media and on social media.
The news agency added that "Iran's plans to break the blockade are certainly being drawn up," but that no one outside the circle of security and military decision-makers had knowledge of them.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed on Sunday at least one incident involving an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, saying military forces had been involved in the encounter.
No further details were released about the identity of the forces involved or whether the tanker had been attempting to circumvent the blockade. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) had not commented on the incident as of Monday.
Also at Monday's briefing, Baghaei was asked how Tehran might respond to reported US planning for a possible attack on Iran.
"The best scenario is for them to get the hell out of the region," he said, adding that IRGC Air Force commander Majid Mousavi would deliver Iran's response to any potential attack "in a neat and elegant package."
Mousavi said on Sunday that IRGC aerospace capabilities had grown since the previous round of conflict and that "the field is ours and we determine the battlefield."
IRGC deputy commander-in-chief Major General Mostafa Izadi said Iran's missile range had been significantly upgraded and that any threat would draw an immediate response "without geographical limitations."
Azizi, chairman of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated the same position, saying Iran had determined it would face no geographical limitations in any future confrontation.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf cited remarks by Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei about the need to end the current situation, saying "sustainable deterrence" was the way out of the crisis.
"We must remove the shadow of war from ourselves," Ghalibaf said. Iran needed to fulfil "the directive of the Supreme Leader" Khamenei, he added.
Baghaei elaborated on remarks by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who said the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within two hours of the other side fulfilling its commitments.
Baghaei said the comment was meant to signal Iran's readiness to act quickly, not to minimise the complexity of a potential agreement.
Tehran's conditions, he said, include lifting US sanctions, ending the naval blockade and implementing commitments Washington accepted under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Trump has described the Islamabad memorandum as a waste of time and declared it null and void, and has characterised ongoing negotiations with Iran as "a load of nonsense".
Diplomatic efforts are continuing despite the standoff. Qatar's prime minister is expected to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday, with Doha serving as a key mediator between Tehran and Washington.

Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Iran will use all tools to confront the naval siege and defend itself.
Iran says it will use all means at its disposal to counter a United States naval blockade imposed during the nine-month US-Israel war on Iran.
The ⁠US blockade was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached ⁠a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.
“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news briefing on Monday.
“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitute an act of military aggression against Iran,” Baghaei said.
“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”
The war broke out on February 28 when the US and Israel carried out air strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.
The conflict has since expanded after Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the region and with armed groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict with Iran continuing in its efforts to block the waterway, which is vital for oil and natural gas shipments.
In an attempt to force Iran to halt efforts to block the strait, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and later announced a series of economic sanctions and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.
Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks that ships have caught fire while trying to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
TankerTrackers.com said last week that a tanker was loading Iranian crude oil in the Gulf via ship-to-ship transfer and could become the first vessel to successfully export the country’s crude since the US reimposed the blockade in July.
Baghaei said on Monday that reports about Iranian ships loading oil are “speculation”.
Visible Iranian crude exports decreased to near zero in recent months due to the blockade.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the US blockade is hurting Iran economically.
“Iranians are aware of that and they are publicly admitting it because more than 80 percent of the country’s imports and exports happen through the Strait of Hormuz or southern ports of the country,” he said.
“Iranians are now looking increasingly for options to put an end to the US naval blockade,” our correspondent said, adding that military action against US military assets around Iran is being discussed.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the war remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June agreement that laid out a path to a permanent settlement.
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days if Washington meets its conditions, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions.
“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” Baghaei said.

Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’
Nine people were shot at a concert in central California , leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.
The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.
One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff’s department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.
Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn’t elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The department didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.
As of Monday, there had been more than 420 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive . The archive, a nonpartisan resources, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed.
High numbers of mass shootings reported annually in the US have prompted many to call for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress over the years has not passed such restrictions.

Retailer says it believes no personal data that could lead to fraud was accessed after hack of third-party supplier
Next has warned that hackers have gained access to data relating to the clothing and homewares retailer through a technology supplier.
The firm said on Monday that it had been informed that one of its third-party suppliers had “experienced a cyber incident” resulting in unauthorised access to the data.
The high street chain said it believed that customers’ personal data had not been compromised and the information affected was “limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next”.
It is understood the data accessed does not include information such as contact details, addresses, passwords or bank details, which could be used to commit fraud.
It said Next’s systems had not been compromised, though it was “affecting the supplier’s environment” in its business.
Investigations into the hack are in progress. Next said in a statement to investors: “Despite the limited and benign nature of the affected data, we are treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities.”
The latest incident comes amid a spate of cyber-attacks against high-profile retailers around the world.
Last week it emerged that a secret UK government cybersecurity operation had warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums.
That came after hackers caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe , with attacks on fridge and freezer control systems in recent months.
Fashion retailers including the owner of Hobbs and Whistles , TFG London, and the online fashion seller Asos have faced cyber-attacks in which customer data was accessed.
Last year, several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer , the Co-op and Harrods , were hit by damaging cyber incidents which affected operations for months.

Watch: Coughing, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
Police are investigating after thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester following an "unknown substance" being released into the crowd.
It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".
One person was taken to hospital while more than 80 people were assessed for "eye and respiratory symptoms", the North West Ambulance Service said.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said a major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
The force said 12,000 people had been evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue.
Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert.
The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.
Joey Howe says he wondered if it was "part of the show" until the smell hit
He said it was like "time stopped in motion" when "there was nothing going on".
"We then decided to go out. People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.
"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."
Howe also claimed security was "poor" and "very relaxed" with "people walking straight in".
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they had fled the venue.
The 23-year-old told the BBC that she went to the exit and saw lads on the bridge which leads into Medlock Square "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.
She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Concertgoers headed home after the performance was stopped by the incident
Malachi Clarke claimed security was "not good at all" at the venue.
The 19-year-old said: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
"Then we were told by a security guard it was chemical-related.
"After an hour or so of the gig being stopped, we were finally told to evacuate the venue."
Emergency services attended the Co-op Live arena in Manchester after a substance was let off in the crowd
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".
Harper, who was at the concert, told BBC Radio 5Live : "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.
"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.
"I saw people getting wheelchairs out...I was fearful it was something even worse."
Forensic officers are at the arena carrying out investigations
Fans at the rapper's other gigs have claimed similar incidents have taken place earlier on his tour.
They reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
Entrances to Co-op Live remain cordoned off, with police officers and security stewards manning the perimeter which is taped off.
Crime scene investigators in white protective overalls have been moving in and out of the building, as work continues to establish the nature of the substance that caused the evacuation.
GMP said more than 12,000 people had been safely evacuated, with several people assessed for side effects.
"Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert," GMP Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said.
She urged anyone who left the event and has since become unwell to attend their local hospital.
"We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we'd like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it."
Don Toliver recently received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy awards (file photo)
She said the declaration of a major incident enabled the emergency services to coordinate a safe response.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," she added.
The ambulance service added: "Decontamination was carried out as a precaution and one patient was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment."
It said several crews attended, including the Hazardous Area Response Team.
Anyone who has since "noticed side-effects or become ill" is urged to seek medical advice.
There was a large police presence at the venue on Monday morning
In a statement, Co-op Live said venue bosses were working closely with police to identify the cause of the incident.
"Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update from GMP," the statement said.
Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig said the major incident had now ended and she thanked emergency services and venue staff for their "professionalism".
"Enquiries into the cause of the incident are ongoing so those affected can get the answers they deserve," she added.
Toliver, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, was performing in Manchester as part of his Nitrous tour.
The 32-year-old musician has received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, including for Best New Artist.

Next said it was informed by one of its suppliers about the incident
Next has said that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier.
The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.
The firm, which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire, said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".
"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.
"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.
"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."
The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness" and was working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.
Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.
In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account , leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.
The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.
In 2025 Marks & Spencer suffered from a major cyber attack which forced it to stop all online sales for about six weeks and led to some empty shelves in shops.

Sadio Mane was named best player at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.
Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Tuesday afternoon sport's highest legal authority, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), will render its judgement on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they won in January against the hosts in Rabat.
The case was heard in early October, and the wait is almost over.
With 66,000 fans creating an electric atmosphere in the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco were chasing their first Afcon title since 1976.
But the final descended into chaos deep into second-half stoppage time.
With the match goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had blown for a Morocco free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a video assistant referee (VAR) review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing that Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled 'Withdrawals', states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team... refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee", they shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, some people, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
Some Senegal supporters were initially convicted of hooliganism offences after clashes during the final but eventually returned home after receiving a royal pardon
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The FSF's appeal was heard in private on 8 October by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
The panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of ​law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas completed the trio.
If the panel had failed to come to a consensus on the case, Cas president Simon will have made the final decision.
Although Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in March that it will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so, if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Senegal walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at ⁠a ​referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.
"This new rule will also apply ​to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match ​to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw lost his job following Senegal's last-32 World Cup exit this summer, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Morocco dugout in January, was dismissed in March.
Whatever the outcome of the case, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy was furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked Senegal, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
While the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Beneath a record-breaking 141-metre rainbow flag unfurled along Avenida Atlântica , revellers turned Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana seafront into a roaring celebration of music, ornate drag costumes and pulsing sound trucks for the 31st Rio Pride Parade , one of Brazil’s oldest. Starting from Posto 5 on Copacabana beach and featuring more than 200 artists staged by Grupo Arco-Íris under the banner "We recognise every form of love and existence as legitimate" , marked 15 years since 10 judges on Brazil’s Supreme Court unanimously ruled on 5 May 2011 to recognise same-sex stable unions as family units with equal rights and duties.
Yet the beachfront euphoria unfolded against a sobering backdrop of persistent hostility: parade coordinator Cláudio Nascimento noted that hard-won judicial milestones, from civil unions and marriage equality to transgender name and gender recognition and the criminalisation of LGBTphobia, have not stemmed day-to-day abuse, with Brazil’s 2026 Atlas da Violência logging 10,250 reports of violence against gay and bisexual people in 2024 ( up 5.5% on 2023 ) alongside a 2.5% rise in cases involving transgender and travesti people. Urging Congress to enshrine court victories into robust legislation and strengthen protections for transgender citizens, organisers made the Copacabana march both a tribute to past breakthroughs and an urgent demand for safety and equality.

After spending 22 hours trapped beneath concrete slabs , 79-year-old Valentyna was pulled alive from the wreckage of a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv , devastated by a Russian drone strike . Found on the first floor, she was handed to paramedics and taken to hospital, offering a rare moment of relief amid the destruction .
Under the glare of floodlights, rescuers searched through mountains of broken concrete and twisted metal , while sniffer dogs combed the ruins for survivors. Emergency workers carried injured residents to ambulances, recovered bodies from the rubble and even brought a cat to safety.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service announced the rescue on Monday, as the death toll climbed to 11 and two people remained missing . The attack, which struck overnight on 22 November, destroyed part of the residential block, leaving emergency crews working through the night in search of anyone still buried beneath the rubble .

A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Senegal are contesting CAF’s decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal winning the final 1-0 in January.
The Court of Arbitration ‌for Sport (CAS) will release its decision on Senegal’s appeal against ⁠being stripped of ⁠this year’s Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title on Tuesday.
Senegal are contesting the decision of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) to declare Morocco champions , despite Senegal ⁠beating the hosts 1-0 in extra time in January’s final in Rabat, and the outcome will be announced on Tuesday, the court confirmed on Monday.
CAS heard the arguments of Senegal, Morocco and CAF in Lausanne ⁠in early October.
It had initially promised a decision within days of the hearing on ‌October 8 but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a CAS Award. That process requires several weeks.
CAS Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. Awards may be enforced by sports federations or state courts, depending on the circumstances.
In the final , Senegal ⁠ walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty ⁠was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.
Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal ⁠scored the winner to secure victory.
However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled ⁠that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off ⁠the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco.
Senegal appealed the CAF ruling to sport’s highest court, CAS, on March 25, but it was heard some six months later. The ‌basis of its arguments is that the referee’s decision is final and he allowed the match to be completed.
The CAS panel is presided over by French sports law ‌expert ‌Gerald Simon, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, Ulrich Haas.

Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, the United States, on Saturday evening, one of them critically, local authorities said, a night of violence that comes as the state reports a decline in killings.
The shooting broke out around 7:30 p.m. local time in Strathmore, a town of about 3,000 people in Tulare County, in California's Central Valley.
Roughly 150 people were at the event, including performers from neighbouring states, when an unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd, according to the Tulare County Sheriff's Department. No arrests have been announced.
The most seriously injured victim is a 26-year-old man shot in the chest, who underwent surgery and remains in critical condition. Two others, aged 19 and 22, also needed surgery. The remaining six victims had minor injuries.
The sheriff's department said it believes the shooting "may be gang-related" but did not elaborate.
Officials said the public is no longer in immediate danger. The department did not immediately respond to further questions.
The attack comes despite a recent fall in violent crime across California. The state reported 1,374 homicides in 2025, a 17.5% drop from 1,666 in 2024, according to the California Department of Justice.

TV8 ekranlarının sevilen yarışması MasterChef Türkiye'de haftanın eleme gecesi geride kaldı. 22 Kasım Pazar günü yayınlanan bölümde eleme potasındaki dört yarışmacı, Danilo Zanna, Mehmet Yalçınkaya ve Somer Sivrioğlu'nun karşısında hünerlerini sergiledi. İki aşamalı mücadelenin sonunda en düşük puanı alan yarışmacı, MasterChef hayallerine veda etti. İşte MasterChef'e veda eden isim...
Eleme gecesinin ilk etabında Şadi, Şükran, Armağan ve Tolgahan'dan ana malzeme olarak yer elması kullanarak yaratıcı yemekler hazırlamaları istendi. Şeflerin verdiği 45 dakikalık sürenin ardından yarışmacılar tabaklarını değerlendirmeye sundu.
İlk turun puan sıralamasında Armağan 21,5 puanla zirveye yerleşti. Şükran 21 puanla ikinci, Şadi 20,5 puanla üçüncü, Tolgahan ise 17,5 puanla dördüncü sırada yer aldı.
İlk turun ardından eleme heyecanı ikinci etapla devam etti. Yarışmacılar bu kez Somer Şef'in "Ben Saksı Değilim" adlı tabağını hazırlamak için tezgah başına geçti. Şeflerin verdiği bir saatlik sürenin sonunda tabaklar yeniden puanlandı.
Değerlendirme sonucunda Armağan ve Şadi eleme potasından kurtulurken gecenin son iki yarışmacısı Şükran ve Tolgahan oldu.
Şeflerin iki etapta verdiği puanların toplamı sonucunda MasterChef Türkiye'ye veda eden yarışmacı Şükran oldu. Tolgahan, rakibinden 1 puan fazla alarak ilk 11'e kalmayı başardı.
Tabağını tamamlayamadığı için büyük üzüntü yaşayan Şükran, elenmesinin ardından gözyaşlarını tutamadı. Böylece MasterChef Türkiye'de 22 Kasım Pazar akşamının eleme gecesi sona erdi.
Şükran, ''Şimdi gideceğimi bilsem bile gene aynı şeyi yapardım. Takım arkadaşlarımla yarışırken aldığım karar gerçekten onların düzeni bozulmasın. Biz küçük toplumda büyüdük. Aman düzen bozulmasın mantığıyla büyüdüğümüz için o niyetleydim. Nasip devreye giriyor. Ben burada çok güzel şeyler yaşadım. Oğluma hatıra bırakmak için gelmiştim. Seyircilerden bir yanlışım olduysa özür dilerim.'' diye belirtti.
Gözyaşlarına hakim olamayan Şükran, ''Onu çok özledim. Ben evde kendimi motive etmek için örgü örüyordum. Hepinize birer tane atkı ördüm. Bugün de o kadar emindim ki kendimden yoksa yanımda getirirdim. O bana terapi oluyordu. Sizleri tanıdığıma çok memnunum oğluma hatıra bıraktım. Burnumun direği sızlıyor. Anneciğim, ben buraya sadece senin için geldim. Sana güzel bir hatıra bırakmak için geldim. İyi ya da kötü bir sürü olaylar yaşadım ama hayatım boyunca tek yapman gereken şey her zaman dürüst olman ve inandığın yolda hep devam etmen yavrucuğum. Bunu izlediğinde umarım çok mutlu olursun'' diye ekledi.

texts.https://www.dw.com/en/after-japan-s-apec:
Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled over Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at last week's APEC summit.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury .
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
"This gives China little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise," he said. "However, this approach comes at a cost to Beijing too: the more it relies on coercion, the more it pushes Japan towards increased defence spending and closer ties with other partners."
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
"I expect Japan to try to find areas where it can signal goodwill and seek to improve relations in return for small-scale compromises, but a reset in the dynamics will be determined by how the Trump administration shapes its foreign policy for the remaining years of his term," Yang added.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.
"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."
"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides."

Yükselişin arkasında ilk sırada Fed'in faiz artırımı beklentilerindeki geri çekilme yer alıyor. Geçen hafta altını 14 ayın en düşük seviyelerine çeken sıkı para politikası senaryosu, yeni haftanın ilk işlem gününde bir miktar yumuşadı. ABD Hazine Bakanı Scott Bessent'in, Fed'in enflasyonla mücadelede aşırı sıkı bir politika izlemesinin ekonomi için risk oluşturabileceği yönündeki değerlendirmesi de piyasaların gündemindeydi.
Yapay zekâ yatırımlarına ilişkin endişelerle küresel hisse senedi piyasalarında yaşanan satışlar, yatırımcıların güvenli liman arayışını artırdı. Haberlere göre tahvil getirilerindeki geri çekilme ve doların bir miktar değer kaybetmesi de ons altına destek verdi.
Cuma günü gram altın 5.731 liraya kadar gerilemiş, ons altın ise Eylül 2025'ten bu yana en düşük seviyelere inmişti. Pazartesi sabahındaki hareket, bu kaybın önemli bir bölümünün geri alındığını gösteriyor. Analistler ise iki yönlü bir tablo çiziyor: Bazı değerlendirmelerde son haftalardaki sert düşüşün şimdilik sona ermiş olabileceği ifade edilirken, kalıcı bir yükseliş için henüz net bir sinyal oluşmadığını söyleyenler de var.
Yatırımcıların bu hafta takip edeceği başlıklar ise belli. Fed yetkililerinin faiz mesajları, ABD 'den gelecek enflasyon verileri ve Aralık ayı faiz kararına ilişkin beklentiler altının yönünü belirleyecek. Dolar endeksindeki hareket ve küresel borsalardaki dalgalanma da fiyatlar üzerinde etkili olmaya devam edebilir. Yurt içinde ise gram ve çeyrek altın, ons altının yanı sıra dolar/TL kurunun seyrine bağlı olarak değişecek.

Altın piyasasında yaşanan sert geri çekilme, hem elinde altın bulunduran hem de alım fırsatı kollayan yatırımcıların yakın takibinde. Rekor seviyelerin ardından düşüşe geçen ons ve gram altında yön arayışı sürerken, Ekonomist Tuna Kaya piyasadaki satış baskısının perde arkasını ve önümüzdeki döneme dair yol haritasını paylaştı. Kaya, gram altın için 13 bin TL rakamını telaffuz etti.
Altın fiyatlarındaki geri çekilmeyi üç ana nedene bağlayan Tuna Kaya, ABD Merkez Bankası ’nın (Fed) aralık ayında yeniden faiz artışına gidebileceği yönündeki beklentilerin güçlenmesinin doları ve tahvil faizlerini yukarı çektiğini hatırlattı. Küresel teknoloji ve yapay zekâ hisselerinde yaşanan sert satışlarda yatırımcıların nakit ihtiyacını karşılamak için altın pozisyonlarını bozduğunu belirten Kaya, petrol fiyatları ve jeopolitik cephedeki belirsizliğin de kısa vadede altını baskıladığını ifade etti.
Mevcut tablonun uzun vadeli yükseliş trendinin bittiği anlamına gelmediğini vurgulayan Kaya, tarihsel döngülerde büyük rallilerin ardından yüzde 25 ile 40 arasında düzeltmelerin normal karşılandığını söyledi. Kısa vadeli al-sat yapanların temkinli olması gerektiğini belirten ekonomist, uzun vadeli birikim yapanlar için ise panik satışından kaçınılması gerektiği uyarısında bulundu.
Piyasadaki geri çekilmenin durulacağı teknik seviyelere işaret eden Tuna Kaya, ons altında 3.450-3.500 dolar aralığının güçlü bir destek bölgesi olduğunu aktardı. Bu bandın altına sarkılması halinde 3.350-3.400 dolar seviyelerinin test edilebileceğini ancak buradan hızlı bir tepki yükselişi beklediğini dile getirdi. İç piyasada ise gram altın için 5.500-5.600 TL aralığının hem teknik hem de psikolojik açıdan kritik bir eşik olduğunu vurguladı.
Kısa vadeli hareketlerde pazartesi ve salı günlerine dikkat çeken Kaya, petrolün 80 doların altına inmesi ve ABD - İran hattındaki tansiyonun düşmesi halinde tepki alımlarının hızlanabileceğini öngördü. Bu senaryoda ons altında 3.700-3.900 dolar, gram altında ise 6.200-6.400 TL bandına doğru bir toparlanma yaşanabileceğini kaydetti.
Kaya, 2027-2028 döneminde ons altının 7.000-8.000 dolar seviyelerine ulaşabileceğini öngördü.
Gram altında ise önce 10.000 TL ara hedefinin, ardından 12.000-13.000 TL bandının gündeme gelebileceğini dile getirdi.
Tuna Kaya, asıl güçlü yükseliş dalgasının 2027 yılının başından itibaren ivme kazanacağını öngördü. Merkez bankalarının rezerv artırma iştahı, küresel borç yükü ve süregelen jeopolitik risklerin altını beslemeye devam edeceğini söyleyen Kaya, dönem bazlı fiyat beklentilerini şu şekilde sıraladı:
2026 Yıl Sonu: Ons altında 3.700-4.200 dolar , gram altında 6.500-7.500 TL aralığı.
2027 Yıl Sonu: Ons altında 4.500-5.500 dolar, gram altında 9.000-11.000 TL bandı.
2027-2028 Dönemi: Ons altında 7.000-8.000 dolar ve üzeri; gram altında ise önce 10.000 TL ara hedefi, ardından döviz kurunun da etkisiyle 12.000-13.000 TL seviyeleri.

Oscar ödüllü ABD'li oyuncu Jennifer Lawrence, rol aldığı filmlerdeki öpüşme sahnelerine ilişkin açıklamalarda bulundu.
36 yaşındaki Lawrence, Andy Cohen'in sunduğu Watch What Happens Live programında birlikte kamera karşısına geçtiği oyuncuları öpüşme sahnelerine göre sıraladı.
Programda kendisine Liam Hemsworth, Bradley Cooper, Josh Hutcherson, Chris Pratt ve Timothée Chalamet arasında seçim yapması istendi.
Lawrence'ın esprili bir dille verdiği yanıt, sosyal medyada gündem oldu.
Sunucu Andy Cohen'in oyuncuları en iyiden en kötüye sıralamasını istemesi üzerine Lawrence, önce "Hepsi çok harikaydı" diyerek yanıt verdi.
Böylece Lawrence, en iyi öpüşme sahnesini Josh Hutcherson ile çektiğini belirtirken Chris Pratt'i listenin sonuna yerleştirdi.
Jennifer Lawrence ile Chris Pratt, 2016 yapımı bilim kurgu ve romantik türündeki Uzay Yolcuları (Passengers) filminde birlikte rol aldı.
Filmde Lawrence ve Pratt, başka bir gezegene doğru 120 yıl sürecek yolculuk yapan bir uzay gemisindeki iki yolcuyu canlandırdı.
Planlanandan yıllar önce uyanan iki karakter, yolculuk boyunca beklenmedik olaylarla karşı karşıya kaldı.
Lawrence ile Pratt'in öpüşme sahnesi de filmin romantik hikâyesinin bir parçasıydı.
Jennifer Lawrence'ın listesinin ilk sırasında yer alan Josh Hutcherson, oyuncuyla Açlık Oyunları (The Hunger Games) serisinde birlikte rol aldı.
Lawrence, seride Katniss Everdeen karakterini canlandırırken Hutcherson, Peeta Mellark rolünü üstlendi.
Oyuncunun ikinci sıraya yerleştirdiği Liam Hemsworth ise aynı film serisinde Gale Hawthorne karakterine hayat verdi.
Lawrence, Bradley Cooper ile Umut Işığım (Silver Linings Playbook) ve Serena filmlerinde, Timothée Chalamet ile de 2021 yapımı Don't Look Up filminde kamera karşısına geçti.

Oscar'lı yıldız Jennifer Lawrence , ekrandaki en kötü öpüşme sahnesi deneyimini anlattı. 36 yaşındaki Amerikalı oyuncu, bu itirafı Andy Cohen'in sunduğu 'Watch What Happens Live' programının yeni bölümünde yaptı.

Esprili bir şekilde, "Hepsi çok harikaydı" diyen oyuncu, "En iyiden en kötüye doğru sıralamak gerekirse, en iyisi Josh'tu. Sonra Hemsworth, Cooper, Chalamet, Pratt geliyor" ifadesini kullandı.
Lawrence, 2016'da Chris Pratt ile birlikte rol aldığı bilim kurgu-romantik film 'Uzay Yolcuları'nda (Passengers) öpüşme sahnesi çekmişti. Filmde ikili, yeni bir yuvaya doğru 120 yıllık yolculuğa çıkan bir uzay gemisinde hibernasyondaki binlerce yolcudan ikisini canlandırıyordu. Ancak yolculuk beklendiği gibi gitmiyor ve ikili, planlanandan onlarca yıl önce uyanıyordu.
Ünlü oyuncu, 'Açlık Oyunları'nda da Josh Hutcherson ile birçok kez öpüşmüştü. Ancak film serisinde bir tek Hutcherson ile öpüşmemiş, Liam Hemsworth'le de öpüşme sahnesi çekmişti.
Lawrence, 'Silver Linings Playbook' ve 'Serena' gibi filmlerde Bradley Cooper'ı öpmüştü.
Ünlü oyuncu, 2021 yapımı 'Don't Look Up' filminde Timothee Chalamet'yle öpüşme sahnesi çekmişti.

Programın on beşinci haftasında eleme potasında Şükran, Tolgahan, Şadi ve Armağan yer aldı. Şükran haftanın ilk eleme adayı olmuştu. Cumartesi akşamı oynanan son dokunulmazlık oyununda takım kaptanı olan Şükran, eşit biten oylamada son sözü söyleyerek Armağan'ı potaya göndermişti.
Danilo Zanna, Mehmet Yalçınkaya ve Somer Sivrioğlu'nun puanladığı eleme iki etap üzerinden oynandı. Yarışmacılar ilk etapta yer elmasıyla yaratıcı tabaklar hazırladı. Bu turu 21,5 puanla zirvede tamamlayan Armağan oldu ve potadan ilk kurtulan isim olarak eleme gecesini geride bıraktı.

Şeflerin puanları açıklandığında Tolgahan, Şükran'ın 1 puan önüne geçerek ilk 11'e kalan yarışmacılar arasındaki yerini korudu.
